name: MCTS-Guided Policy Improvement for Combinatorial Outputs
key_paper: Wang, R., et al. (2024). EfficientZero V2: Mastering Discrete and Continuous Control with Limited Data. arXiv:2403.00564. Preprint (no venue listed as of Aug 2025). Primary predecessor: Schrittwieser, J., et al. (2020). Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model (MuZero). Nature 588, 604-609.
algorithm_description: MCTS-guided policy improvement uses Monte Carlo Tree Search as a planning oracle that refines a neural network policy's action proposals via lookahead simulation. The policy network (actor) proposes candidate action distributions, which seed MCTS rollouts from the current state; the visit-count statistics from MCTS simulations produce an improved target distribution (pi_MCTS) that is typically sharper and better than the raw network output. The actor is then distilled toward pi_MCTS via KL-divergence minimization, completing the policy improvement step. A learned world model predicts next states and rewards so that MCTS can simulate trajectories without real environment interaction. EfficientZero V2 extends this framework to both discrete and continuous action spaces with explicit data-efficiency improvements: priority replay, Siamese self-supervised consistency loss, and careful hyperparameter scheduling allow training from as few as 100K environment frames rather than the millions required by original MuZero.
action_space_handling: Standard MCTS-guided policy improvement operates over a flat discrete action space (single categorical choice per step). For combinatorial set outputs (choose k distinct items from {1..N}), the action space is expanded to one of two representations: (1) Factored autoregressive MCTS — each of the k selection steps is a separate MCTS node level, and the search tree has depth k; at step t, the policy masks already-selected items and MCTS searches over the remaining N-t candidates. (2) Joint exponential space — all C(N,k) subsets are enumerated as flat actions; impractical for N=50, k=7 (approximately 99 million combinations). The autoregressive factored approach is the only tractable option for lottery-scale N and k, and maps naturally onto sequential MCTS tree expansion with masking at each ply.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: Under the autoregressive MCTS formulation, each play of k numbers is built step-by-step: at step t (t=0..k-1), the policy network outputs logits over {1..N} with already-selected indices masked to -inf; MCTS runs from this state using the policy as a prior, accumulates visit counts via UCB1/PUCT exploration, and the visit-count distribution over unmasked candidates becomes the improved target. The selected number is sampled (or argmax-selected) from the MCTS visit distribution; the chosen number is appended to the running set and the next step begins with an updated mask. After k steps, exactly k distinct numbers have been selected. Alternatively, if a learned world model is available, MCTS can internally simulate multi-step lookahead of the remaining selections using the world model's predicted states, evaluating candidate subsets before committing to any choice.
sequential_generation_strategy: MCTS-guided policy improvement is inherently sequential/autoregressive when applied to combinatorial outputs: each number selection is one MCTS decision step, conditioned on all previously selected numbers via the accumulated mask. This means inter-number correlations are fully modeled — the policy can learn that selecting ball 7 at step 1 makes ball 14 or ball 21 more or less likely at step 2 (e.g., based on historical co-occurrence patterns in draw data). This is a strict improvement over flat joint multi-hot generation which treats each ball independently. The cost is k forward passes through both the policy network and the world model per play generation, and a search tree of depth k per play at inference time.
gradient_estimator_type: MCTS-guided policy improvement does not rely on REINFORCE or reparameterization gradient estimators in the standard sense. The policy is trained via supervised distillation: the MCTS visit-count distribution pi_MCTS serves as a soft target, and the loss is a KL divergence (or cross-entropy) between pi_MCTS and the current policy output pi_theta. This is a direct regression target rather than a sampled policy gradient — gradients flow through a differentiable cross-entropy loss, making training stable and low-variance compared to REINFORCE. The value function is trained via TD-learning (n-step returns from MCTS value estimates). This distillation-based update is the key reason MCTS-guided methods are more stable than raw policy gradient on small data: the MCTS target provides a low-variance, planning-improved supervision signal rather than a high-variance Monte Carlo reward gradient.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Combinatorial constraints (exactly k distinct from {1..N}) are enforced via autoregressive masking within the MCTS tree: at each tree node representing step t, the valid action set is restricted to {1..N} minus already-selected indices. MCTS expansion only considers valid (unmasked) actions, and the policy prior is renormalized over valid candidates before computing PUCT scores. This guarantees exact k selection with no duplicates by construction. No post-hoc rejection sampling is needed — the constraint is baked into the MCTS action space at every node. The world model also only needs to predict transitions over valid actions, simplifying the state representation (the current partial set plus the step index t).
sample_efficiency_rating: low-to-medium. MCTS-guided methods like EfficientZero V2 dramatically improve sample efficiency over model-free RL (PPO, DQN require millions of frames; EfficientZero V2 achieves comparable performance in 100K frames on Atari). However, '100K frames' still far exceeds 100-200 lottery draws. The core challenge is that the learned world model requires sufficient state-action-reward transitions to generalize — with only 100-200 draws, the world model will overfit severely and produce hallucinated rollouts that mislead MCTS. If the world model is replaced by a hand-designed lottery simulator (historical draw replay as environment), MCTS-guided improvement becomes more feasible but degrades to replaying historical data, eliminating the lookahead advantage. Rating: low for fully learned world model on 100-200 draws; medium if world model is simplified to a historical-replay oracle.
regularization_built_in: Several regularization mechanisms are inherent: (1) MCTS smoothing — MCTS visit counts naturally smooth the policy target, distributing probability across multiple plausible actions rather than collapsing to a single argmax; this acts as implicit regularization against mode collapse. (2) Dirichlet noise at MCTS root — standard AlphaZero/MuZero adds Dirichlet noise to the root prior to encourage exploration during MCTS, providing stochasticity that prevents deterministic policy collapse. (3) Self-supervised consistency loss (EfficientZero V2) — a Siamese representation consistency objective regularizes the encoder, critical for small datasets where supervised signal alone is insufficient. (4) L2 weight decay on the policy and value networks. (5) Value target clipping and n-step return truncation prevent outlier rewards from dominating. (6) KL-based policy distillation loss is inherently soft and avoids hard argmax targets, providing label smoothing similar to knowledge distillation.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Critical failure modes with n < 200 draws: (1) World model hallucination — a learned transition model trained on < 200 draws produces unreliable state predictions; MCTS lookahead through a broken world model yields confidently wrong value estimates that mislead the policy distillation step. (2) MCTS depth vs. data tension — deep MCTS trees require many reliable rollouts; with few training samples, simulation quality degrades rapidly with lookahead depth. (3) Value function overfit — the critic memorizes return statistics of the small training set; MCTS backpropagation propagates these overfitted values upward, amplifying overfit through lookahead. (4) Exploration collapse — without sufficient experience, MCTS explores poorly and converges to a narrow set of candidate actions; Dirichlet noise alone cannot compensate for severely limited training data. (5) Computational overhead without benefit — MCTS is expensive per inference step; on small data with an unreliable world model, the computational cost is not justified by improvement over simpler policy gradient methods.
data_regime_evidence: EfficientZero V2 (Wang et al. 2024) benchmarks at 100K Atari frames (~2,000 episodes of 50 steps each), which is substantially more than 100-200 lottery draws. Detailed analysis: (1) minimum_training_samples_tested: EfficientZero V2 reports results at 100K, 200K, and 500K frames on Atari — the 100K regime is the closest to small-data, achieving near-human performance on many games. However, even 100K Atari frames involve far more state diversity than 100-200 lottery draws (which are all sampled from the same stationary distribution). (2) performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] — EfficientZero V2 does not publish a curve for performance vs. training samples in the 50-500 range; published ablations stop at 100K frames. AlphaZero-like methods require millions of self-play games even in board games with perfect simulators. (3) comparison_baseline: EfficientZero V2 outperforms DreamerV3, IRIS, and TD-MPC2 at 100K frames on Atari; all baselines still require far more data than 200 samples. No evidence of validation at lottery-scale data volumes in the literature.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: No finite-sample convergence guarantees exist for MCTS-guided policy improvement with learned world models at n < 200. Theoretical foundations: (1) AlphaZero converges to optimal policy in self-play given a perfect simulator and sufficient compute (Silver et al. 2018, no finite-sample bound). (2) MuZero/EfficientZero convergence depends on the quality of the learned world model; with a misspecified model (inevitable at n < 200), convergence to the true optimal policy is not guaranteed — the method can converge to a locally optimal policy under the model's incorrect dynamics. (3) MCTS with UCT has logarithmic regret bounds in tree search given a fixed bandit problem (Kocsis & Szepesvari 2006), but this applies within a single search tree, not to the overall policy optimization loop. (4) In practice, MCTS-guided methods require extensive hyperparameter tuning (simulation budget, c_puct, Dirichlet alpha) to converge reliably — these are validated empirically, not theoretically, and the optimal settings differ substantially across problem regimes.
reward_distribution_handling: MCTS-guided methods handle sparse rewards through value bootstrapping and n-step returns within the search tree: MCTS propagates value estimates up the tree via backpropagation, effectively computing multi-step return estimates. For a lottery reward structure (95% zero-reward plays): (1) Reward scaling — raw hit counts (0-7) are typically normalized; near-all-zero rewards cause value estimates to collapse near zero, providing weak gradient signal. (2) Distributional value (MuZero Reanalyze variant) — a distributional critic can be used instead of a scalar value to capture the shape of the sparse return distribution, retaining information about the rare high-reward events. (3) Priority replay — EfficientZero V2 uses prioritized experience replay that over-samples rare high-reward transitions; this is directly beneficial for lottery-like sparse rewards, ensuring the few positive-reward draws are replayed frequently. (4) Minimum draws for stable learning: MCTS-guided methods need a sufficient number of non-zero reward samples to calibrate the value function; with only 5-10 non-zero reward plays in 200 draws, value function training is severely data-limited. Practical minimum: 500+ draws for stable value learning with MCTS.
credit_assignment_granularity: Standard MCTS assigns reward at the episode/play level — a single scalar reward is backpropagated through the search tree at terminal nodes. For lottery application: (1) Play-level credit is default: the reward (number of hits, 0 to k) is assigned to the entire k-number play and propagated backward through the k-step MCTS tree. (2) Step-level credit within MCTS: because the autoregressive MCTS tree selects numbers one at a time, each selection step can in principle receive intermediate rewards. A shaped intermediate reward (e.g., +1 if the number selected at step t appears in the actual draw, 0 otherwise) provides number-level credit assignment directly within the MCTS lookahead, similar to semi-bandit feedback. This is a significant advantage over flat play-level methods: MCTS can naturally incorporate number-level feedback without architectural changes, simply by providing step-wise rewards during tree expansion. (3) This makes MCTS-guided generation one of the few methods that can natively exploit number-level semi-bandit feedback in the combinatorial setting.
diversity_mechanism: MCTS generates diverse plays through several mechanisms: (1) Dirichlet root noise — at the root of each MCTS tree, Dirichlet-distributed noise (alpha=0.3, epsilon=0.25 in AlphaZero) is added to the prior policy, ensuring stochastic exploration across different number combinations for each play generated. (2) Temperature-scaled visit count sampling — after MCTS, action selection uses a temperature parameter tau to sample from visit counts rather than taking argmax; tau=1 early in training transitions to tau->0 for exploitation at inference. (3) Multiple independent MCTS trees — generating N plays requires N separate MCTS search instances from the same root state; each tree accumulates independent random noise and produces a different play. (4) Explicit play diversity constraint (custom extension) — a diversity reward penalizing overlap between simultaneously generated plays can be incorporated by treating batch play generation as a multi-agent MCTS problem. The Dirichlet noise and temperature combination is the primary diversity mechanism and is well-established in AlphaZero/MuZero literature.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: MCTS-guided policy improvement with a learned world model is primarily designed for online or near-online settings where the world model can be continually updated from real environment interactions. Compatibility with offline lottery-nn constraints: (1) Offline via model-based RL — the world model can be trained entirely on historical draws and frozen; MCTS then simulates rollouts using this fixed model without additional real draws. This enables offline policy improvement but inherits all world model overfit problems on small data. (2) MuZero Reanalyze (Schrittwieser et al. 2021) allows replaying historical data through the current world model to generate fresh value/policy targets — this is a form of offline MCTS that is more data-efficient. (3) Historical replay as simulator — treating the draw history as a finite replay environment and replaying MCTS from past states; fully offline but limited by the 100-200 historical draws. Verdict: MCTS-guided methods can be adapted to offline settings but require a reliable world model; with 100-200 draws and a weekly draw cycle, the world model training data is insufficient for reliable offline MCTS. Operationally feasible only if the world model is simplified or replaced by domain knowledge (e.g., a frequency-weighted lottery simulator).
key_dependencies: PyTorch (already present). No standard off-the-shelf MCTS-guided RL library handles combinatorial set outputs natively. Useful libraries: (1) mctx (Google DeepMind's JAX MCTS library — JAX, not PyTorch, port required); (2) muzero-general (PyTorch MuZero implementation, GitHub); (3) torchrl (Meta's RL library with some MCTS support); (4) Custom MCTS implementation is typically needed (~300-500 lines). Additional: numpy, scipy for Dirichlet sampling. No pip-installable complete solution as of 2025.
estimated_lines_of_code: 700-1000 lines of new code: MCTS tree data structure with PUCT scoring (~200 lines), world model (transition + reward + representation networks, ~200 lines), autoregressive combinatorial action masking within MCTS (~100 lines), policy distillation training loop with value targets (~150 lines), Dirichlet noise and temperature sampling utilities (~50 lines), replay buffer with priority sampling (~150 lines), integration with SharedLotteryTransformer backbone (~100 lines). Excludes evaluation harness and logging.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Medium-to-high compatibility with the existing SharedLotteryTransformer. The encoder serves as the representation network (h_theta) that maps draw sequences to latent states for MCTS. The existing actor head can seed the MCTS prior policy. However, MCTS-guided methods additionally require a dynamics network (g_theta) that predicts the next latent state given current state and action — this is entirely new and cannot be derived from the current architecture. The reward prediction head is also new. The encoder and policy head weights from the pretrained backbone provide a strong initialization for the representation and prior networks, significantly reducing the training burden. Overall: the backbone is reusable for 2 out of 4 required networks; the dynamics and reward prediction networks must be trained from scratch on the lottery draw data, which is the highest-risk component given data scarcity.
specific_application_in_project: In lottery-nn, MCTS-guided policy improvement would be used in Phase 3 (or a late Phase 2 extension) as a planning-enhanced play generator. Concretely: (1) The SharedLotteryTransformer encoder becomes the representation network h_theta encoding the sequence of recent draws into a latent state z. (2) A lightweight dynamics network g_theta predicts the next latent state z' given z and the number selected at each MCTS step t (simulating 'what if we chose ball i next?'). (3) A reward predictor r_theta estimates the expected hit count for a given state-action pair. (4) At play generation time, for each of 5 plays: run MCTS from the current state with k=7 plies deep, masking previously selected balls at each ply; sample from the visit-count distribution for each step. (5) After each real draw, MuZero Reanalyze replays historical draws through the current world model to generate updated policy/value targets and retrain. The primary benefit over simpler methods (REINFORCE, PPO) is the lookahead capability: MCTS can evaluate candidate number combinations multiple steps ahead, potentially discovering synergistic combinations (co-occurrence patterns) that one-step policy gradient methods miss. However, given only 100-200 draws, the dynamics network is the critical bottleneck — it must generalize from very few transitions. Recommended: prototype first with a simplified hand-designed simulator (frequency-weighted random draw as 'world model') before training a learned dynamics network.
integration_point: Phase 3 (probabilistic models, DeepAR, N-BEATS) — too complex and data-hungry for Phase 2 given current dataset size. Could be revisited as Phase 2 late addition if dataset grows to 300+ draws.
replaces_or_extends: Extends the existing SharedLotteryTransformer by adding a dynamics network, reward prediction head, and MCTS planning loop on top. Does not replace the encoder backbone. Replaces temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py with MCTS-driven play generation. Extends rather than replaces the Actor-Critic framework — MCTS provides the policy improvement operator instead of PPO's clipped surrogate.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. muzero-general (https://github.com/werner-duvaud/muzero-general) — PyTorch MuZero implementation for Atari/board games; does not support combinatorial outputs but provides the core MCTS + world model framework. 2. EfficientZero (https://github.com/YeWR/EfficientZero) — original EfficientZero PyTorch implementation; Atari-focused, no combinatorial action support. 3. EfficientZero V2 — no official public code release confirmed as of Aug 2025 (paper is arXiv preprint); community re-implementations may exist. 4. mctx (https://github.com/google-deepmind/mctx) — DeepMind's JAX MCTS library with MuZero and AlphaZero implementations; JAX only, requires port to PyTorch. 5. open_spiel (https://github.com/google-deepmind/open_spiel) — supports MCTS for combinatorial games (combinatorial game theory), some Python bindings; not RL-in-the-sense-of-policy-gradient but useful for MCTS scaffolding. 6. No lottery-specific or set-selection MCTS reference implementation found as of Aug 2025.
benchmark_results: EfficientZero V2 benchmarks (Wang et al. 2024): Achieves human-normalized median score of ~194% on Atari-100K (100K frames budget), compared to ~105% for DreamerV3 and ~153% for IRIS at the same budget. On continuous control (DMControl suite at 100K steps), EfficientZero V2 achieves state-of-the-art on 12/16 tasks. Original MuZero (Schrittwieser et al. 2020): superhuman on Go (2840 Elo), Chess, Shogi, and Atari — with millions of self-play games. AlphaZero (Silver et al. 2018): combinatorial game (Go, Chess, Shogi) policy improvement via MCTS with millions of games. Key limitation for lottery-nn applicability: all published MCTS-guided results assume a reliable simulator (perfect for board games, learned but validated for Atari); no published results on combinatorial set selection from {1..N} with k distinct elements and n < 500 training samples.
notable_use_cases: 1. Board games (AlphaZero, MuZero) — MCTS as policy improvement operator for combinatorial game trees (Go has branching factor ~250, qualitatively similar to choosing from N=50 balls). 2. Combinatorial optimization with MCTS — MCTS applied to TSP and graph coloring, where each step selects one node from remaining candidates (structurally identical to autoregressive ball selection with masking). 3. Drug discovery / molecular design — MCTS guided by a GNN policy for molecular fragment assembly, selecting chemical building blocks sequentially from a fixed vocabulary; sparse reward (biological activity), combinatorial output — the most structurally similar use case to lottery-nn. 4. Chip placement (Mirhoseini et al. 2021, Nature) — RL with lookahead for combinatorial placement decisions; demonstrated feasibility of RL on combinatorial design with limited labeled data via reward shaping. 5. Recommendation slate generation — MCTS applied to sequential item selection for k-of-N slates, with diversity rewards; structural analog to generating multiple lottery plays with diversity constraints.
